The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. This is the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide - a designation which requires evidence of country's intent to destroy a national, racial, ethnic or religious group in whole or in part. Myanmar argued it was responding to attacks by insurgents, but the court said the scale and nature of its actions went "well beyond" what was required. 

The ICJ does not have any power to enforce its rulings, but this historic decision has been welcomed as a symbolic victory by Rohingyas and human rights groups. Some analysts have said it could have bearing on future allegations of genocide, including the case brought by South Africa against Israel over the war in Gaza.

author: BBC News
description:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping have held historic talks in the Shenzhen, China - the first time they have ever held a private three-way meeting together.

In the joint statement from China, Russia and the US, the three leaders committed to a dialogue on "reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation".

In the meeting, Xi said nuclear weapons "should be comprehensively banned and completely destroyed" and a "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."

description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority population in northern Rakhine state.
 
In 2017, a military crackdown killed thousands of Rohingya - a Muslim ethnic minority - and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar for neighbouring Bangladesh.
 
Judge Yuji Iwasawa says there is a "reasonable inference that Myanmar security forces acted with genocidal intent", and Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya.
 
Myanmar had denied genocide in the case brought by The Gambia.

author: BBC News
description:
Communities around the UK could face the same fate as a flooded Welsh village if work is not done to manage the risk of underground mine water, the BBC has been told. 

Families in south Wales whose homes were submerged by a torrent of mine water after a quarry blast said they now fear their children could be caught in another flood. 

With a quarter of people in the UK living above old mines, experts in flood risk management and mines have said more needs to be done to assess the risk from flooding and protect families and their homes. 

The UK Government said there is no "national assessment" of the risks posed by flooded mines, although various bodies do have responsibility for some mines. 

The owner of the quarry in Wales, Breedon, said it recognised the distress the flood caused but said it was an isolated incident following a project that was years in the planning. It added it is cooperating fully with the HSE investigation.
